_comentario: MODELO TEENS. Aula IMPAR = modelo de FALA (REGRA 29): dialogo line-by-line + 3 role-plays, sem texto central. Vozes iguais as aulas 1-4: 'ellen' remapeada para voz de adolescente (12 anos), 'candy' para a segunda voz jovem (Ruby), 'arthur' intocado para as palavras soltas do Word Arena e para o adulto do listening 2. lesson.menu_desc: A friend who has never been here asks what your street is like -- relative clauses, defining and non-defining -- 24 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- New City, New Street
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Sophia | Lesson 5 -- New City, New Street
lesson.grammar_point: relative clauses: defining, non-defining and reduced

listenings.text: When we moved, it was only four miles, but it felt like another country. On my old street there was a bakery on the corner which opened at five in the morning, and the woman who ran it knew everybody's name. There were children my own age in every building, so I was never inside the house. The new street, which looks nicer in photos, had nothing on the corner at all, and for the first month I thought there was nobody here my age. Then I met a girl walking a dog that never stops barking, and it turned out she lives two floors below me. So the street I hated in March is the one I would not leave now. It did not change. I just met the people who were already in it.

Welcome to the neighborhood walk. The whole route is six blocks and it takes about forty minutes at an easy pace. Start at the square behind you. On this first street you will pass the building with the green door, which is the oldest one here, and a bakery that has been in the same family for three generations. Now, on the second block, look for the crosswalk painted in yellow. The park you can see from there is the one everybody uses at the weekend, though it gets crowded after ten. The last street, which most visitors miss, has the small market where people who live here actually do their shopping. Take your time, and mind the traffic at the corner.

items.situation: Your friend asks what is near your building. Answer with one sentence, not a list — put a relative clause in it.
tips: There's a bakery on the corner that opens at five in the morning.
There's a park two blocks away which gets crowded at the weekend.

items.situation: Describe the doorman to somebody who has never met him. Use a non-defining clause.
tips: Jorge, who has been here longer than we have, knows everything about the building.
Jorge, who is the doorman, has worked here for twenty years.

items.situation: Say what changed about your street since you moved in.
tips: My street, which used to be very quiet, is full of cars now.
The avenue behind us, which they closed for a year, has just reopened.

items.situation: Name a place without naming it: describe it with a relative clause and let your teacher guess.
tips: It's the place where you buy bread.
It's the thing that takes you to the metro.

items.situation: Your friend asks whether anything is open early. Ask them back about their own street, with a relative clause.
tips: Is there anything near you that opens before eight?
What's the place everybody goes to at the weekend?
